set.summary: Between late 1947 and 1949 most Palestinian Arabs in the territory that became Israel fled or were expelled; the UN describes the result as the permanent displacement of more than half of the Palestinian population. Contemporary estimates of the number of refugees include 472,000 (UN Mediator, 1948), about 711,000 from Israel-controlled territory (statistical expert of the UN Conciliation Commission, 1950) and about 750,000 Palestine refugees whom UNRWA served when it began operations in 1950. Israel made any repatriation conditional on a formal peace settlement, and the refugees and their descendants became UNRWA's caseload.

displacement.note: UN Mediator 472,000 (1948); UNCCP 711,000 (1950); UNRWA about 750,000 served in 1950

set.summary: The day after the declaration, forces of Egypt, Transjordan, Syria, Iraq and Lebanon entered the former Mandate territory; Transjordan's Arab Legion operated mainly in areas allotted to the Arab state and in the Jerusalem zone. For the whole 1948-49 war, the Jewish Virtual Library's casualty table gives 6,373 Israelis killed and an estimated 10,000 Arabs killed, a combined estimate for Palestinians and the Arab armies.

affected_populations.note: JVL estimate combining Palestinians and the invading armies; all Arab figures are estimates.

set.summary: In the 'Ten Days' between the truces, Operation Dani captured Lydda, Ramle and the airfield. On 12-13 July the remaining inhabitants were expelled toward Arab Legion lines: the Institute for Palestine Studies puts the number at about 70,000 including neighbouring villages; many died of thirst and exhaustion on the march. Palestinian sources put those killed inside Lydda at more than 400, including at the Dahmash mosque, and the total including deaths on the march at close to 1,000. An unspecified number of Israeli soldiers were also killed in the capture of Lydda.

affected_populations.note: Palestinian sources: more than 400 killed inside Lydda, close to 1,000 including deaths on the march; IPS about 70,000 expelled.
Source: 'A number of Israeli soldiers were killed'; no figure in opened sources.

set.summary: At the end of October 1948 the IDF launched an offensive that took the Upper Galilee from the Arab Liberation Army under Qawuqji and pushed into southern Lebanon. The UN Mediator's representative reported that some 25,000 additional refugees had been forced out of Galilee.

affected_populations.note: Some 25,000 additional refugees forced out of Galilee (UN Mediator's representative, FRUS 3 Nov 1948).

set.summary: To house the flood of new immigrants, ma'abarot - immigrant absorption camps - were set up in the 1950s, replacing the less habitable immigrant camps and tent cities. They began to decline by the mid-1950s and many were transformed into development towns; the last closed in 1963.

In 1964 the National Water Carrier, built by Mekorot, began pumping water from the Sea of Galilee to the centre and the northern Negev. Arab states saw it as diverting Jordan basin water; the Arab League launched a headwaters diversion plan, and Israeli-Syrian armed clashes over the Arab diversion works followed from late 1964 to 1966.

In response to Fatah attacks launched from the West Bank, the IDF mounted a large daytime raid on the Jordanian-held village of as-Samu, demolishing about 125 houses, the village clinic and a school, and fighting Jordanian troops. UN observers were given death certificates for 14 Jordanian soldiers and 3 civilians and medical certificates for 37 soldiers and 7 civilians wounded; a US estimate put the dead at about 50, half of them Jordanian soldiers. Israel did not give its casualty figures to the UN observers. The Security Council censured Israel in Resolution 228, and unrest in the West Bank against King Hussein followed.

affected_populations.note: Jordanian army personnel: UN S/7593 death certificates for 14 (a captured Jordanian major also died in Israeli custody); US estimate (FRUS) about 25 soldiers.
Civilians (as-Samu/Hebron area, then Jordanian citizens): UN S/7593. 125 houses, the clinic, a school and a workshop demolished; 28 houses and a mosque damaged.
Israel declined to produce its casualties as witnesses to UN observers (S/7593).

set.summary: Israel's population grew from 806,000 in 1948 to 1,578,000 at the end of 1951, mostly through immigration of Holocaust survivors from Europe and of Jews from Arab and Muslim countries, with an Israel State Archives table counting 377,251 immigrants from Muslim countries between May 1948 and the end of 1952, as communities in Iraq, Yemen, Libya and elsewhere left amid hostility and legal pressure. Absorption strained housing, food supplies and the budget.

add_cite.claim: Israel State Archives table: 377,251 immigrants from Muslim countries, May 1948-end 1952

set.summary: After infiltrators from the West Bank killed a mother and her two children at Yehud, IDF Unit 101 under Ariel Sharon raided the Jordanian-held village of Qibya, blowing up some 41-50 houses (UN observers counted 41 dwellings and a school) and killing 69 villagers by the commonly cited count (UN observers reported 53 at the time), many of them hiding inside. The raid was condemned internationally, including by UN Security Council Resolution 101.
